speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: ROSSLAND, B.C.-REPORTED DECISION TO REMOVE STATION AGENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday as reported at page 1129 of Hansard the hon. member for Kootenay West asked the following question:
In view of the recent decision of the board of transport commissioners to remove the agent from the station at Rossland, a city of over 4,000 population, and in view of the strong protests by the city council, the chamber of commerce and the population of that city, would an appeal to the governor in council against this decision receive consideration?
The governor in council is always prepared to consider any reasonable appeal against

an order or decision of the board of transport commissioners. However, in considering appeals to the governor in council from orders of the board there has been a long standing practice not to disturb such orders unless it is clearly evident that the board has acted upon some wrong principle or has otherwise erred. Where the matters at issue are questions of fact, such as in the Rossland case, and are questions that the board is qualified to determine and which it has determined after holding hearings, it has been customary not to interfere with the findings of the board which has been constituted a court of record for the determination of such questions of fact.
In the Rossland case a district inspector of the board was sent to Rossland to investigate. A public meeting was held there on November 2, 1961, and interested parties were heard. It was shown that the Canadian Pacific Railway had established a merchandising service depot at Tadanac, about six miles from Rossland, in June, 1961, with pick-up and delivery trucking services to Rossland and that, in consequence, practically all traffic is now being handled by truck with delivery in most cases direct to the consignees. Carload traffic outward from Rossland was nil in the last reported year, and incoming carload traffic averaged about 12 cars monthly in that period.
The board considered that in view of the reduced traffic since the establishment of the merchandising services, the burden to the company of maintaining the agency outweighed the modest public loss and inconvenience resulting from closing the agency. The board therefore ordered the closing of the agency.

I should like to give a word of explanation with regard to vote No. 615, which we are considering at the present time. This vote covers the $190,000 required to reimburse the provinces of Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba for one half of the amounts expended by them under emergency fodder bank programs instituted during the drought last summer. It will be recalled that on August 30, 1958 the Prime Minister advised the house of the government's intention to consider assisting provinces in the establishment of forage bank programs under which farmers would receive certain incentives to put up forage as a reserve against an emergency situation.
During July, 1961 an offer was made by the government to the three prairie provinces to pay half of a bonus of $5 per ton to farmers making cereal fodder available to fodder banks. The purpose was to encourage farmers to salvage as fodder, cereal crops which would not likely produce economic yields as grain. Each of the three prairie provinces established a fodder bank program on a municipality basis. Farmers consigning cereal fodder surplus to their requirements to a municipal fodder bank were eligible to receive a $5 per ton bonus.
The volume handled under the program was approximately as follows: Manitoba, 7,600 tons; Saskatchewan, 65,200 tons and Alberta, 2,000 tons. This vote will cover Canada's share of the program, which is $2.50 per ton.

This has been a very worth while program. As has been pointed out,

Fodder coming into this country is subjected to a tariff levy. I do not have the precise amount in mind; it is not a large levy, though I think it is in excess of $1 a ton; I may be mistaken. that a farmer receives under this program on an average, on a acreage basis, if he takes advantage of this program under which the provincial and federal governments will each pay $2.50 per ton in respect of his fodder. In northern Ontario we were very interested last year both in this scheme and in the operation the government was carrying out in connection with food banks, especially in view of the fact that in northern Ontario we had a large amount of hay which was not going to be used this year. I suggested to the Department of Agriculture that this hay could be assembled at a reasonable price and the government could provide a subsidy for shipments of hay moving between eastern and western Canada or from the northern areas of the prairie provinces to parts of the country where transportation costs are prohibitive. I do not think we should have to bring in hay and fodder from the United States.
That was not my suggestion at all.

I did not say it was anyone's suggestion. In view of our transportation facilities and the control we exercise over them it should be possible to limit the disastrous effects of drought in western Canada.
Through the exercise of various controls it was possible to prevent a widespread throwing on the market of hay and fodder. The suggestion has been made in my area that in times of drought cattle could be moved to northern Canada for government supervised pasturing and wintering on a basis similar to that applicable in community pastures. I think this would be a step in the right direction. Natural disasters occur in all segments of the agricultural industry from time to time. There are sources of hay and fodder in northern Canada, and those areas happen to be on the way to the markets to which cattle is usually sent. Much of the cattle from western Canada moves into the Toronto and Montreal markets. I advance this suggestion for consideration.
Will the minister tell us whether the sums involved in this item represent a contribution to alleviate conditions produced by drought last year, or is this a regular fodder program for western Canada? I also wish to know how the federal government arrived at this sum of money. Does the federal government contribute at the request of the provincial government? To what extent does the federal government control or participate in the distribution of the fodder once it is in the fodder bank? Is its distribution supervised, and has the government any say as to who receives the product? Probably some advantage would flow from an interprovincial exchange of the assembled product. Does the

administration of the program by the federal government make this possible?

Mr. Chairman, the administration of this program is entirely on a provincial and municipal basis. This is merely a subsidization of the provincial governments for what they have done in this program.
This brings me to a question asked by the hon. member for Assiniboia as to how much applied to which province. The figures are as follows: Manitoba, 7,600 tons amounting to $19,000; Saskatchewan, 65,200 tons amounting to $163,000; Alberta, 2,000 tons amounting to $5,000, for a total of $187,000. The item is actually for $190,000, but that is about as close as we can safely come to an estimate.
I am grateful to the hon. member for Assiniboia for his suggestion regarding import duty. Consideration was given to the importing of feed and hay duty free, but the implications in several provinces were such that it was considered best to try to overcome this problem by further assistance in the affected areas.
I was asked about the program of assistance for Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba. In accordance with the terms and conditions prescribed by the Minister of Agriculture the federal government pays one half the amount paid by those provinces in respect of the transport of fodder and feed in the period of this fiscal year. That is covered by another item of $1.5 million which was passed in supplementary estimates No. 1 of the current year.

I thank the minister for his reply. I am very disappointed that the minister has not been able to say that in this time of crop failure emergency farmers living along the United States boundary are allowed to go what is often just a few miles across the border and supplement their supplies by bringing in feed from the United States duty free. It is obvious to the minister that if you live in the centre of a province you can travel 30 miles in any direction and stay within the province, but if you live within five or six miles of the United States border and there is feed available in the United States, that is the handiest source.
I think it is a bad practice for the government not to allow farmers living along the border to bring in supplies from the United States in times of emergency without paying tariff. I can tell the minister that farmers living along the border feel they should be allowed to do so, not as a long term policy but in an emergency. They appreciate the action taken by the government with respect to general trucking costs and the assistance provided through this item, and so on, but

I share with them the feeling that it is ridiculous to deny them the opportunity of bringing in supplies from the United States, the most economical source, duty free. Those who are acquainted with the situation along the border feel, as I do, that the farmers there have a legitimate claim for repayment of the duty they have already paid.
I think the government should have another look at this question. I believe the farmers have a legitimate claim to be reimbursed the amount of the duty. They did not go across to the United States to buy fodder because they wanted to go there or because they preferred to go there. They went over there only because of crop failure the previous year.
Why was it cut off in the first place? Because the farmers wanted it.

If my hon. friend wishes to object to what I am saying, that is fine. The farmers who live in his part of Saskatchewan will know that he has objected to what I am saying. However, I am saying that the producers who live along the United States boundary feel that this is the rankest kind of discrimination in what could be an emergency year. I think the minister should check with his colleagues and persuade them, if he can, to reimburse these farmers for the duty which has been paid and which is a great hardship and a tax that should not be levied in that emergency situation. How does it make any sense at all to say that we will put an item in the estimates in order to help them overcome a difficult situation, but that for those who live along the boundary we will maintain a tax in order to make it more difficult for them to meet this emergency situation.

I perhaps left the wrong impression with my friend the hon. member for Assiniboia. I did not mean to say that I think anything in this world is final and irrevocable for all time. I was explaining what the situation is at the present time and the problems of adjusting duties which are, as he knows, applied to the country as a whole. There are difficulties, but this is not to say that I will not see that another look is taken at this matter in order to ascertain whether some adjustment might be possible.

If I may I should like to say one further word. Perhaps the best action would have not been to remove the tariff. I do not know about that matter; I am not an administrator. Perhaps the way to handle it is to reimburse the people who have paid the tariff if they submit a claim. But whether
Supply-Agriculture
it is handled in one way or another, I submit that it is gross discrimination against the farmers who live along the boundary for them to be charged a duty when they are going a few miles from home in order to supplement greatly needed fodder reserves. I think it is contrary to the government's policy in other ways. I think it is contrary to the government's natural desire to prevent a glut of cattle on the market. In order to be consistent, I think the government should follow the suggestion I have made, even though some other members may not agree with what I have said.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I should like to ask the minister this question. Can he inform me whether the government of the province of Ontario made a request for assistance to the farmers of northern Ontario who, owing to very bad weather last season, had a poor crop of hay and grain? Was any request made by the government of Ontario to have assistance given jointly with the federal government?

I believe not. I am not aware of any, in any case.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, I am glad the minister has agreed to examine the proposal which has just been made by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) concerning the abolition of customs duties on animal feed imported from the United States.
Farmers in eastern Canada also have a problem with respect to the importation of certain feed grains, especially com, oats and barley. Consequently, I would ask the minister-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. I have the impression that the hon. member is straying too far afield. I would ask him to limit his remarks to the item under consideration.

Mr. Chairman, we are now speaking of subsidies in respect of the crop and the baling of feed cereals, and I think that, with regard to the feeding of animals, grain is also a food. As the minister answered the hon. member for Assiniboia-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If I have rightly understood the hon. member, he was just about to deal with an entirely new matter. Therefore, I ask him to limit his remarks to the vote mentioned in supplementary estimates No. 3. As a matter

Supply-Agriculture
of fact, the subject matter of this debate should not be extended so as to become a general discussion on agricultural problems. I therefore ask the hon. member to comply with standing orders, which are very clear.

Mr. Chairman, I would simply ask the authorities of the Department of Agriculture to check whether or not customs tariffs on cereals might be eliminated for imports from the United States intended for western farmers. On the other hand, if this suggestion is considered, I fail to understand why we should not analyse the possibility of doing the same for the eastern farmers in this country.
We should not forget that our eastern farmers are also liable to crop damage. Indeed, last year, as the hon. member for Cochrane (Mr. Habel) just said, farmers in northern Ontario lost part of their crop, and if I remember correctly, the Ontario farmers association asked the federal government for assistance. I even think that a newspaper in northern Ontario-and I would like to be corrected if I am not right-published an item which stated that the federal government had not acceded to the request for assistance made by the northern Ontario farmers.
I reiterate my request to the effect that the Department of Agriculture examine the possibility of abolishing customs tariffs on imported cereals intended for eastern farmers.
(Text):

I am certainly not happy with the remarks that have been made here, particularly by the last two speakers. We have a surplus of hay in northern Ontario, and we are not asking for any relief. We do not want any relief. However, my farmers of northern Ontario are paying this subsidy to western Canada. I think we have the right to ask the government to keep this money in Canada, at least, and not to go along with this proposal that the stuff be allowed to come in from the United States duty free. If our people are going to pay this assistance, then I think we at least have the right to ask that this assistance be put in another form so that the hay can be transported and there may be an equalization of the supply between eastern and western Canada.
The hay in northern Ontario, when delivered in the province of Manitoba with the freight rate that is now applied, will not cost as much as the Manitoba government paid last year in order to go to the United States
[The Chairman.]
and bring hay into that province. It is my understanding that they paid $34 last year for a limited quantity of hay. I feel quite sure that the ridings of Cochrane and Timis-kaming can supply hay to that area at a lower price than that. If we give some assistance-and there is no objection to giving this kind of assistance-then I think we should at least be fair to the rest of the Canadian farmers, and should not ask them to subsidize something for the advantage not of their own farmers but of United States farmers. If we are going to put the matter on an assistance basis, let us at least keep it in Canada and let us try to help all the farmers in the various parts of Canada where-ever it seems to be advantageous or even possible to do so.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I noticed that the hon. member stated that northern Ontario had a good crop of hay. I am glad to know that in his riding such may have been the case last year. I also note that he took exception to the remarks I made. In doing so he showed that he knows little about my riding. The farmers in my riding will certainly understand that he does not give much consideration to farming in my district. The farmers of my district are in dire need of assistance, and they have been asking the Ontario government to come to their aid. We are not opposing this amount at all. We are absolutely in favour of it. I simply asked the minister whether any requests had been made by the government of Ontario, and the answer was no. That goes to show that the government of Ontario has little interest in the riding of Cochrane, and I can see that the hon. member for Timiskaming is very little interested in the riding of Cochrane.

Mr. Chairman, I am not going to speak for the riding of the hon. member. His farmers have the advantage of being a little closer to the western market than farmers in my riding, and I presume there would be an advantage from the point of view of freight rates from his area as compared with mine.
I am in no way disagreeing as to the need for assistance. We need assistance in my riding because for the last three years the farmers have not been able to sell their hay. I am only suggesting that when there is a great need in western Canada, the farmers of Cochrane might also like to be able to sell some of their hay to western Canada. I am simply opposed to the setting up of conditions providing for the importing of hay from the United States rather than using the money involved to bring about an equalization of the supply and demand in Canada for the benefit of our farmers. No matter how you look at it, even those farmers in the hon. member's riding of

Cochrane north, who are in very serious circumstances will have to pay toward this assistance, and I think they should be given the opportunity to sell the hay they produce if it is to the advantage of the Canadian economy and will not cost any more money. I object to us paying any money to assist farmers in another country while there is still a great need in our own country and a supply of hay available. I believe the matter could be worked out if consideration were given to it.
This is not something new. I have raised the matter with the Minister of Agriculture; I have telephoned him several times. The department discussed the matter and looked at the price. I think I am being fair in saying that in the early days of the drought in Manitoba some of the officials there thought there was not going to be enough hay available, and panic buying of a limited quantity of hay brought about a very high price. Because of the high price we made the suggestion that assistance be given with respect to transportation costs so that hay could be moved from northern Ontario, where I am informed by the farmers there is a surplus. It is only with this in mind that I am opposed to the lowering of the customs barriers, because obviously the money involved would come out of the Canadian treasury and our Canadian farmers would not necessarily be assisted.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: I want the hon. member to know that the farmers of Cochrane riding-he referred to it as Cochrane north-would be well satisfied to take all the hay they need from the hon. member's riding if they had the assistance of the province and the federal government. As a matter of fact they need it badly.
Mr. Chairman, I think the last two speakers have been talking about two other problems with which this item does not deal.
We are paying for this.

Let me explain. The hon. member for Timiskaming said that we could bring the cattle down through northern Ontario on the way to market. The cattle for which the feed was required were breeding stock. The feeders were all shipped out of western Canada as soon as possible. With regard to the surplus of hay in northern Ontario and other parts of that province, as a result of the plan implemented by this government there was no shortage of fodder in western Canada. Under the plan implemented by the government, crops that would not yield more than three bushels per acre were cut for fodder. Consequently there was enough fodder left on the prairies for the
Supply-Agriculture
requirements. In fact in my own constituency, which I believe was one of the hardest hit in Saskatchewan, I visited many municipalities with regard to the program implemented by the government and in not one municipality was the demand for fodder greater than the amount that had been cut for that purpose in that municipality.
The hon. member for Assiniboia talked about the importation of fodder from the United States. It was the farmer's own decision whether he went to the United States, brought in hay and paid the duty or whether he went to northern Saskatchewan and paid the extra cost of hauling. In addition, it was as a result of the farmers' request in the first place that the duty was imposed, so that hay would not come into Canada from the United States in good times. They cannot have it both ways.
I think they can in an emergency. This is a special case.
There was not the emergency that the hon. member says there was. Fodder was available in Saskatchewan, and they could have obtained it there.

The best source of fodder for the people in this area was the source closest to home. In certain instances the fodder closest to home was in the United States, but if they went 10 miles from home across the United States boundary they had to pay a duty which simply increased the amount of money in the Canadian exchequer, and I claim this is definitely discrimination in an emergency.
How many tons were involved?
Mr. Chairman, I did not realize that land rehabilitation and irrigation came under this item.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No, they come under the next item, No. 616.

Item agreed to.
Irrigation and water storage projects in the western provinces including the South Saskatchewan river project; the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act program; land protection, reclamation and development-
616. Construction or acquisition of buildings, works, land and equipment-further amount required, $3,200,000.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make a brief statement on item 616 by way of explanation to the committee. Because of the severe drought conditions that prevailed in the prairie provinces throughout 1961 there was an unprecedented demand for assistance in the development of individual

Supply-Agriculture
farm and community water conservation projects and to provide pasture and feed facilities. Almost twice as many small farm water projects as in any previous year, consisting of dugouts, stock watering dams and small irrigation projects, were constructed to help to meet the critical situation. In addition, more of the larger community storage projects were constructed than planned, and an emergency federal-provincial-municipal well drilling program was initiated last fall to provide water for communities. Under this program the federal and provincial governments each contribute 35 per cent of the cost of a well and the municipality 30 per cent. Some 100 applications for such wells have been approved to date.
More community pasture facilities and more feed bases had to be provided in those areas most affected by the drought to preserve farmers' basic herds and reduce unseasonable marketing. This was accomplished by constructing a large community pasture of 140,000 acres in the British block in Alberta and a smaller one in Manitoba. These projects were not anticipated for 1961-62. In addition, a feed base for several hundred head of cattle was set up at Craven, Saskatchewan, where pelleted grain screenings were fed at a nominal cost to the farmers.
As a result of the situation created by the drought it is estimated that expenditures will exceed the amount provided in the main estimates by $1 million under the small water development program and by $100,000 under the community pasture program. The balance of the additional amount of $3,200,000 required consists of $500,000 for the St. Mary's irrigation project in Alberta and $1,600,000 for the South Saskatchewan dam.
Construction of the Waterton dam on the St. Mary's project was started in 1960 and will be completed in 1962. The South Saskatchewan dam was started in 1958 and will be completed in 1965. The additional amounts mentioned for the projects for 1962, totalling $2,100,000, are required because the works in progress advanced at a faster rate than expected. This was largely due to the abnormally dry season, which made it possible for the large earth-moving contracts to be carried out without interruption. The constant dry weather also helped to speed up the work on other contracts, although not to the same degree as the earth-moving contracts.
I should like to emphasize, Mr. Chairman, that these further amounts do not represent increases in the total cost of these projects. We are merely advancing into this fiscal year money that it was originally expected

would not be required until the next fiscal year. I might add that the amount for this item in the main estimates for this fiscal year was $18,322,297.

I should like to say a few words on this particular item and on the importance of an irrigation and water storage program, not only to the area I represent but to the whole of the fertile Red river valley and to the western provinces. The serious drought experienced by the prairie provinces last year points up the necessity for an extensive program of land and water conservation. In my own area the farmers are appreciative of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, and this tremendous program of building farm dugouts and dams is one of the most important undertaken by the federal Department of Agriculture.
Experience over the years has shown us that these water storage programs will pay large dividends in the development of our prairie economy. In my constituency the spring water running down the streams and rivers from what we call the Pembina escarpment is largely lost to that particular part of the country. The building of dams in this area is a definite must if the fullest development of our agricultural economy is to be achieved.
Further to this, I should like to express my appreciation of the fact that this is recognized not only by the government of Manitoba but by our own federal Department of Agriculture. I should also like to express my appreciation of the auspicious start that has been made on this program in our area in the building of the Stephen-field dam on the Boyne river, which will be started this spring. I sincerely believe that a continuation of the program of water storage will turn out to be one of the most important developments in prairie agriculture. We only have to listen to the figures the minister gave a few moments ago to realize how this development is being encouraged, not only by the governments of the prairie provinces but also by the federal government. I am sure all members will join me in saying that this is one of the most important developments to take place, and one which will probably be taken over by ARDA to make land and water rehabilitation a reality.
(Translation):

Mr. Chairman, we certainly have no objection to the adoption of those items since they will hasten construction of the dam on the Saskatchewan river and the carrying out of other irrigation projects.

In the past, we have often said that the scope of this measure should be widened so that all Canadian farmers could benefit from it. We would like it to have a bearing on the whole of Canada.
I appreciate that western farmers are to benefit from this measure; it is justified by the farmers' water supply and especially by the construction of the dam on the Saskatchewan river.
However, if we consider the possibilities resulting from the irrigation of the land along the Saskatchewan river, we find that there will be half a million more acres of farmland once the projects are completed and the irrigation system is installed.
I understand that this area will be used to produce grain crops and also, perhaps, feed crops, but more especially grain crops.
No doubt that the Saskatchewan river dam project will then be justified, because it will enable us to produce more grain to help supply the foreign markets, which should still be large enough at that time.
I should like to ask the minister to keep in mind our suggestion that the possibility of extending this measure to all provinces be examined. While our problems may not be the same as those of western Canada, they do exist. In the east, our problems relate mainly to soil drainage and stone clearing. Much of our land could be made suitable for agriculture if it were cleared of stones and well drained. The cost of such undertakings would not be too high.
I understand that, in 1962, there will probably be appropriations for ARDA, but for the time being we cannot anticipate that measure, because the minister, who has been talking about it for four years, has never voted the necessary estimates. There is nothing in the speech from the throne to indicate that the government intended to further extend the application of that measure.
I am sure that eastern farmers will be happy when these estimates are voted for western farmers, but just the same, they would be still happier if the measure were extended so as to cover the whole of Canada. (Text):

Mr. Chairman, vote 616 of the
further supplementary estimates asks for an additional amount of $3,200,000 to be divided between two aspects of the department. As
Supply-Agriculture
I understand it, the original estimate was in the neighbourhood of $18 million, which amount we are now being asked to increase. It is my understanding that because this involves an increase of over $3 million in a general estimate, we can discuss briefly certain aspects of general policy as applied not only to what is asked for in the supplementary estimates but also in general under the item of the general estimates.
I am particularly interested in the wording of the first section of vote 616, the heading of which is "Land rehabilitation, irrigation and water storage projects". This is followed by "Irrigation and water storage projects in the western provinces..." As the committee knows, I come from the province of British Columbia, and sometimes I cannot help wondering what the government classifies as the western provinces. I am rather inclined, especially in view of the original vote and the supplementary item, to think there is a great tendency to believe that the western provinces of Canada end at the Rocky mountains, forgetting that the Rocky mountains are just a geographical, mountainous boundary between Alberta and British Columbia.
Admittedly the most westerly province is divided by four mountain ranges, but within those mountain ranges are a number of valleys. These valleys have to a great extent in the past required for their agricultural development-and they require it now-exactly what is set forth as the heading of the supplementary estimate we are now considering, namely land rehabilitation, irrigation and water storage projects.
I have had the privilege of living in British Columbia for 52 years. During that period of time I can remember that the interior of British Columbia was once tantamount to being a desert, growing nothing, but because of water storage and irrigation we now have the most beautiful and agriculturally productive area of Canada known as the Okanagan. However, there is still a great deal that can be done in the way of land rehabilitation and irrigation and water storage projects, shall I say between the city of Armstrong and the town of Osoyoos. I now wish to deal with an area which I know well but which is better known by the hon. member for Kootenay West. I refer to the Creston area, where not too many years ago it was not a matter of irrigation but of land reclamation. This area is now one of the most productive in that part of British Columbia.
The Minister of Agriculture mentioned a few minutes ago that we have a general expenditure of $18 million, and we now have a supplementary estimate of $3,200,000 in connection with land rehabilitation, irrigation and

Supply-Agriculture
water storage projects. In view of these estimates I think the committee will understand why I rise in my seat and ask why it is that, whether it be under the general estimates or the supplementary estimates, the government thinks that Canada ends at the Rocky mountains. I maintain that with proper planning of projects and expenditures my province could give a greater productive return than perhaps any other province. I do not object to any money that is spent in any province of Canada, but why are we so completely and totally ignored in this matter of irrigation, water storage, land reclamation and rehabilitation?
I ask this question not only because I am a member from the province of British Columbia but from my knowledge of the whole of Canada, and particularly, after 52 years, my knowledge of my home province. What is the policy regarding land rehabilitation, irrigation and water storage projects as far as the government is concerned? Why is it that we have been ignored, and is there any possibility or any hope at all of this government raising their sights and looking over the Rockies to that paradise of Canada on the Pacific coast, the province of British Columbia? Our province does not only produce forest and mineral products; it is also an agricultural producer with a potentiality that could give magnificent returns to the benefit of the economy of Canada and the greater security of our people if the program of rehabilitation, reclamation, irrigation and water storage is applied to it as it is rightly being applied to the provinces mentioned by the Acting Minister of Agriculture and those hon. members who spoke earlier.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to express to the Department of Agriculture my satisfaction for last year building two dams on the La Salle river, namely at Starbuck and La Salle. In addition, the contract has now been awarded for the building of a third dam at Elie.
The La Salle river passes very close to the Assiniboine river, and requires that a high level of water be maintained. This can only be done by the diversion of water from the Assiniboine to the La Salle river. This could be done in many ways; it could even be done just by pumping. I understand that a floodway is being constructed, and a great deal of water could be sent through the Assiniboine river during the dry season in the summer to maintain a high level of water in that river. It would be a very easy matter to divert some of this water to the La Salle river, which is not very long. There are farmers all along its course. In some areas these farmers depend entirely on the La Salle river for their water supply in the summer and even in the winter.

Mr. Chairman, before resuming my seat I should like to again express my satisfaction for the speedy manner in which the department has dealt with this problem.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to make one or two suggestions arising out of the well drilling program undertaken this year by the government. This program was really appreciated by the farmers on the prairies, and particularly by those in my area. These farmers feel the program should be extended in the future and should perhaps become as widespread as the dugout construction program in the P.F.R.A. areas of western Canada. In many areas the dugout is not a suitable source of supply for water and a well is a more reliable source, especially when livestock are kept. I should like to express to the minister and to the government the appreciation of the people of Birch Hills and the surrounding area for the large storage and flood control project which was undertaken on Cromarty creek in the railway municipality of Birch Hills. I believe it will be an addition to that area, and that the people will be happy with it.
I believe the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska said he would be happy if P.F.R.A. were extended to the people of eastern Canada. Well, if we go back to the time when that act was first brought in and, later, to the time when its benefits were somewhat extended, we find that the Liberals forgot eastern Canada in the legislation of that day. Now, under the ARDA program, the present government has remembered that there are farmers in eastern Canada who are interested not only in conservation but in the development of projects of this kind. I do not like to say anything more in that regard. However, each time the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska gets up he says "We are happy to see this thing pass, but we would like some of the benefit for eastern Canada as well". I would point out that some of these provisions were made necessary in western Canada because we experienced drought there; perhaps they did not have a drought in eastern Canada.
Too much wind out there in the west. It dries everything up.

I see the man who wants to sell freedom with wheat is speaking now. I know the farmers of western Canada will appreciate that remark.
The Saskatchewan river dam project is, of course, an important one and this year, after we have had a drought in western Canada, everyone out there realizes just how important it is. They also realize that had it been proceeded with at a time when many

people were giving lip service to the idea it might already have proved of great value to people in areas represented by the hon. member for Assiniboia, the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek, the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar and others in Saskatchewan.

I had not intended to take any part in this discussion, but I do not think I can let the remarks of the hon. member for Rosthern pass without a word of comment. The hon. member said the Liberals had ignored eastern Canada. He would not say that in the presence of the hon. member for Cumberland or the hon. member for Westmorland, because each of those members knows what was done about maritime marshland drainage, which was begun immediately after the war by the previous Liberal government. The hon. member is apparently unaware of the legislation which was put on the statute books when Mr. Winters was the minister responsible for the department of resources and development with respect to water conservation in other parts of eastern Canada.
I should like to say a word of appreciation for the work which was begun by the late James Gardiner in assisting pilot projects for the drainage of the bogs in Newfoundland.
I am glad the present government are continuing this work and I hope they will see fit to extend it much more widely. We do not encounter the problem of drought very often, though we did last year. Normally our problem is that we have too much water: we would be glad to have the hon. member for Rosthern come down and cart some of it away.
Notwithstanding the fact that my hon. friend from Drummond-Arthabaska is quite right in pointing out that these programs should be extended to all parts of the country, it is wrong to say that the Liberal government neglected the east. Of course, in the days of the dust bowl when P.F.R.A. was started it was an urgent national problem in the sense that these other problems are not. We all know that one of the reasons the dust bowl has not returned is the splendid work done by P.F.R.A. in all the years since.

I want to congratulate the minister on the able way in which he is dealing with estimates with which he has not had the opportunity of close association. He is an acting Acting Minister of Agriculture.
I know there is really not such a post, but he is acting minister in the absence of the acting minister. This government has become known as a government of travelling cabinet ministers. It is a government composed of
Supply-Agriculture
cabinet ministers who are able to engage in many extracurricular activities.
We heard about your travels yesterday.

At this particular stage, when an election is not too far away the practice seems to be more prevalent than it has ever been. However, I did not know that this practice was extending to parliamentary secretaries as well. Now the acting Acting Minister of Agriculture is fortified with two parliamentary secretaries to the Minister of Agriculture. But I have been looking around for them all the morning-

I do not think the hon. member wants to be unfair. I think he missed what I said when the first vote was called. At that point I explained the absence of the two parliamentry secretaries to the minister. One is in the veterans hospital here; I think it is not too serious a matter, but it prevents his being in the house. The other is absent because of the death of a close relative.

I apologize. I am sorry for having started along that line, and I thank the minister for interrupting me and giving me this information before I was in the embarrassing position of having said something for which I would be sorry. I hope the parliamentary secretary will soon be out of the hospital and, of course, we are sympathetic toward any colleague who has suffered a bereavement in the family.
Now I come to the item under discussion. I want to say, along with the hon. member from Rosthern, that one of the features of this vote which should be given special consideration at this time is the whole question of deep water wells. The program of dams and dug-outs has been well developed over many years, and the experience in this field is considerable! However, the experience with deep water wells is relatively new. This is a new field which has been pioneered. One of the many reasons why deep water wells are now much more feasible than in the past is the fact that the vast majority of farms on the prairies are now supplied with electricity, which makes these wells exceedingly practicable as a source of water supply for livestock.
As the minister has said, this has been an emergency program brought forward to provide under this item for the drilling of deep water wells in a joint program in co-operation with the provinces and the municipalities. It should be made clear that these deep water wells have not been drilled for individual farmers, but are what are called community wells. I take it they are public property, the property of the municipality, although federal and provincial government money has gone

Supply-Agriculture into their construction. All farmers have access to these so-called community wells.
I understood the minister to say the cost was divided on the basis of a 35 per cent contribution on the part of each of the two major governments and a 30 per cent contribution on the part of the municipality. This is only a detail which the minister is free to check, but I understood the division of cost was on the basis of 374 Per cent, 374 Per cent and 25 per cent. One of us is right and one wrong, and probably the minister is right.
The latest information I have is that this program will end on March 31. If there has been an extension I wish to hear about it, and if not I plead with the government to extend this valuable addition to a long term water conservation program at least to the forthcoming full fiscal year, if not permanently. If there was a valid reason for drilling wells in the emergency drought during the past year, the same reason would apply to extending this excellent program in the coming fiscal year. All the federal government can do is make the offer, and I plead with the government to negotiate with the provincial governments for a continuation of the program if not on a permanent basis at least for the coming year, as a minimum extension.
I wish to advance a second proposal. Joint programs are the best. I urge the government to introduce a federal-provincial-municipal program to assist individual farmers to obtain deep water walls. Such a well represents an expensive undertaking. A dugout may be obtained for $500 or $600, but deep water wells often cost $1,000 or $2,000 or more. I wish to be fair to the minister and the government. I have discussed this question with departmental officials at both the federal and provincial levels. The federal government and the government of Saskatchewan both make the same reply to this suggestion. They say it is an excellent one in which they would like to participate, but they are afraid it would lead to their subsidizing, with the assistance of the individual farmers, a group of inexperienced fly by night drillers of deep water wells who are more interested in making a profit than in providing efficient wells. Apparently it is a problem to find competent, reliable drillers in this intricate field, and of course it is difficult for the individual farmer to assess the reliability and competence of a driller.
The federal government could perhaps arrange through the provincial governments for the licensing of drillers on the basis of their qualifications. What I am about to say comes within the purview of provincial government jurisdiction. Perhaps the provincial government could provide a few drilling outlets as pilot undertakings so experience could be

gained in the field. If the provincial government obtained a few rigs and operated them in that kind of work there would be immediate control over the operation and there would be the additional advantage of experience in the field being gained.
In my judgment deep water wells are no longer a luxury. They provide an excellent and convenient source of water for livestock. They are often necessary if farmers are to enjoy the sewer and water advantages so long enjoyed by those in urban centres.
I am not being critical of the minister, as I know he will appreciate. This is an excellent program as far as it has been developed. There are technical difficulties readily admitted by those in the federal and provincial departments of agriculture. This seems all the more reason for providing leadership and taking action so that at an early date not only communities but individual farmers may have the advantage and convenience of deep water wells for the watering of livestock and family use on the farm.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to speak on this subject, but I shall now call it one o'clock.
At one o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

I was trying very hard, Mr. Chairman, to get to my feet before lunch but I could not make it. The various members who have spoken have been talking about their homeland or where they came from and they made me think of a school poem:
Breathes there the man, with soul so dead, Who never to himself hath said,
This is my own, my native landl
Apparently they were all from their native land. I come from the constituency of Cariboo which is as large as the state of Texas. We have everything. We have oil, gold and silver. In fact, a man from this country took $3 million in gold out of Cariboo camp. We have a great deal of oil. We have thousands of men working in the oil fields. The only problem is to get a market for the oil. We have agriculture which compares favourably with the best in Canada. The Peace River area, that gem in the tiara of diamonds, is situated in my constituency. Anybody who has ever been there comes back. We have had people leave and go to California but they came back to the

Peace River country. It is the most prosperous part of Canada right today. I do not say this in any idle way. We have mixed farming which compares favourably with that in the best parts of Iowa or Indiana. The farmers have cattle yards. We had a bumper crop last year. We were not in a part of Canada which was dry and about which all the discussion has taken place. However, we are short of water. We are obliged to dig extremely deep wells. The town of Vanderhoof is in the constituency of Cariboo, and the well went dry there. I think dirt fell in it or something of that kind. However, the government came right to the rescue and dug another well. It was necessary to go to a depth of 500 feet or 600 feet. The whole town was out of water until they obtained this well. I was there and saw what they were doing. The government came right to the assistance of the town.
I think this government is to be congratulated on the way in which they have handled the water situation. Our country was dry. We had very little rain. However, we had a wonderful crop. Another rain would have made all the difference in the world. We had 40 bushels to the acre on the average through there, and a great deal of feed in the form of alfalfa that we could have shipped out. However, apparently nobody wanted the feed. A few carloads were shipped out, but we had hundreds of carloads that could have been shipped out. To give the Minister of Agriculture credit, I think he did a wonderful job in keeping the cattle from being rushed on to the market. In this way the price was kept right. Many people would have gone broke had they been obliged to throw their cattle on the market as was done back in the old days. We were raising cattle and the grass was burned out in the early days. There was no feed in the country. It was grass country. The grass got burned and we were obliged to sell our cattle. We received $12.50 a cow with a good calf thrown in. You do not make much money under those conditions. This year, however, we had plenty of crop but, as I say, we were short of water. For our water supply we depend on dugouts or scoopouts. The government had various units in there, digging these scoopouts. It is not necessary to pay spot cash for them, it Is possible to pay for them on terms.
What any farmer would ever hold against this government is beyond me. I have been in that country for 50 years. We lived in there in the old days under the Liberal 26207-1-774
Supply-Agriculture
regime and it was absolutely the worst one that has ever been seen so far as the farmer is concerned.
He was the forgotten man.

That is true; he was the forgotten man. However, this government apparently see the farmer and have done everything they could to help him. I will tell you this, Mr. Chairman, I would not be here if it was not for the assurance that they will win again. They will win easily in that country. As I say, the Minister of Agriculture has done a wonderful job and we are getting lots of water out of the scoopouts. I have had a letter from my riding saying that we have had snow but the ground is black. We will have a snowstorm one night and chinook winds will come along and fill all the gullies with water. As I said, and I am not boasting, it is the most prosperous part of Canada and it makes my heart bleed when I see these farmers in this part of Canada. There was talk about moving people from the maritimes. We could have taken a lot of those fellows. We have an empire there, and there is not only farming but the farmers have oil wells. Everything is prosperous there.
I am not going to blow too much about my riding because I do not believe it needs any support. When the president of the Fraser Valley association was there at the convention the other day he said that his brother and he were dreaming of getting to the Peace River. They are growing strawberries or something like that, and he said that he and his brother had to get out there. That is their dream. I see my friend the lobsterman smiling, but we have plenty of cattle feed and things will be very prosperous there this year.
As I have said, I do not know why anybody would vote against such a government.
I believe we have leading us the greatest statesman since confederation. I was angered a little the other day when a speaker on the other side was lambasting the Prime Minister because I do not like to see a good man knocked. I would not lambaste one of them if I thought he was any good. Yes, it made my heart bleed when I heard this member lambasting the Prime Minister. Our grandchildren in years to come will be told about this famous statesman. He is going to continue as Prime Minister. He will be returned to office because the people of western Canada-I do not know anything about Quebec-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister; Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: The same thing.

-will not turn him down. He has done more for western Canada than

Supply-Agriculture
any other man. This government has done a wonderful job with regard to the water situation in the Peace River and Cariboo district. They have been digging dugouts and scoop-outs. We have five big scoopouts at home on the farm and they are designed so that one will pump into another. We do not irrigate but there is irrigation in the Cariboo. It is a wonderful part of Canada. It is prosperous and doing well, and so I will not say any more.

Mr. Chairman, I always enjoy listening to the expert on barbershops, barbecues and bulls. He always makes a very interesting address with a lot of homespun wisdom in it. However, in view of the development of the debate on this item I cannot resist saying a few words because of the philosophy of this group which is based on the conservation and development of human and natural resources. On that account this is an important item so far as this group is concerned.
Before proceeding further, I want to support the remarks of the hon. member for Vancouver East and the other members who have spoken in favour of the extension of the application of the policy contained in this vote for land rehabilitation, irrigation and water storage projects. I mention this because there is a particular need in British Columbia which is of increasing importance. Only a few days ago the minister of agriculture for British Columbia, Mr. Richter, addressed the British Columbia fruit growers association in Vernon and stressed the importance of preserving every acre of the 2 per cent of our land suitable for agriculture and settlement. In that address he said that we cannot spare a single acre in British Columbia or destroy a single acre.
I hope the Minister of Justice will keep that in mind when he is contemplating the flooding of about 50,000 acres in east and west Kootenay if the Columbia treaty goes through as now arranged.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.
Are you in favour of the development of the Columbia river?

I am in favour of the development of the Columbia river without any unnecessary destruction of natural resources. I mention this because in British Columbia we have the climate and the soil. I am not blowing like the hon. member who preceded me or even exaggerating when I say that in our district we have numerous farmers who take $1,000 a year in produce per acre off their land year after year. I can think of one

vegetable grower, a neighbour of mine, who lives about nine miles from me. He takes up to $15,000 a year gross from nine acres of beautiful black muck soil beside the lake.
I think of another who takes close to $40,000 off 100 acres and I know of another who takes over $37,000 off 300 acres. I know of numerous fruit growers who take an average of $1,000 a year in peaches and cherries from their orchards which average five acres in extent.
I mention this to emphasize the value of good land in circumstances such as ours and in the Okanagan, where water can be used on a vast scale if it is properly stored in the first instance and diverted to use for Canadian agriculture. Without any partisan approach whatever, I emphasize that there is a great opportunity for the government to make this a national policy and to conserve and develop this land.
Mind you, this is a natural field for government. This is something that cannot be done unless there is government action on the federal and provincial levels. It is something that is beyond the capacity of private interests or, shall I say, beyond the normal sphere of private interests, and there is a wonderful opportunity here for a national policy based on the principles of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. In connection with my statement that I think government action is required, I wish to quote very briefly from the excellent compilation of background papers of the resources for tomorrow conference held in Montreal from October 23 to October 28, 1961. One article is entitled, "Objectives and organizational arrangements for multipurpose development and management of water resources" and it reads in part as follows:
Water development and management In accord with the objectives and value standards of modem society will increasingly depend on governmental action. A variety of forces at work in modern society suggest that more and more emphasis will be placed on intangible values. This tendency, combined with the economic characteristics of water resources, underscores the necessity of relying primarily on governmental institutions to achieve the objectives of water development and management.
In British Columbia water development and management are very closely related to agriculture. In the constituency which I have the honour to represent there are thousands of acres of rich land that could be brought into cultivation if they were drained, for instance, if the Duncan river were lowered six feet by dredging, and there are thousands of acres that can be brought into cultivation by irrigation. There is a far greater acreage that can be brought into cultivation by irrigation in the ridings represented by the hon. members for Okanagan Boundary and Okanagan-Revel-stoke.

There is a tremendous opportunity here so I urge that, particularly in connection with power potential and land rehabilitation, we do not just look at water resources from the point of view of kilowatts and power, necessary as they may be. I think the two can be developed together without any unnecessary destruction of land, which is growing more valuable every year with the increase in world population, and without any unnecessary, shall I say, giving away of water resources that will be required to irrigate this land in British Columbia and the prairie provinces.
Once again I say that in British Columbia we have the climate, we have the soil, and all we need is an extension of this type of legislation so that we could conserve that soil by irrigation, by drainage and in other ways.

I did not intend to take part in this debate, but there were one or two things said this morning which I could not allow to go unchallenged. We are in what you would call the dry belt of Saskatchewan, where last year the dugouts went dry. This government increased up to $240 the grants to farmers for the purpose of constructing these dugouts and also for assisting municipalities in digging deep wells. These wells will be for public use. In our immediate vicinity we have to go down between 400 and 500 feet, and we get artesian wells. We have one well in our vicinity that flowed at the rate of 45 gallons a minute and it served the people for miles around.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate made one statement which I cannot allow to go unchallenged. He said that the former administration had made a great study of the Saskatchewan river dam. I was a member of a committee out west which met the hon. member when he came out west, and we had met with every minister of the former administration who came west during the last 20 years to put this project before them. We met the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate in Moose Jaw, and he said, "We have bogs in Newfoundland that we could drain and bring into production at a cost of $65 per acre, whereas your project, Saskatchewan river dam is costing $3,000 an acre". Well now, 500,000 acres at $3,000 an acre comes to around $1,500 million. If you allot all the costs pertaining to the dam to irrigation alone, you will find you arrive at a figure which is less than one fifteenth of that figure he gave. I cannot, therefore, allow the statement to go unchallenged that he made a study of the Saskatchewan river dam when, out of the blue sky, he could pull this
Supply-Agriculture
figure and give it to these committee representatives who had been promoting this project for the last 15 years. I am sorry the hon. member is not in his seat so that he could reply to that statement.

I congratulate the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Henderson) who managed to speak for 20 minutes without dealing with the subject under discussion, that is, the estimate for $3.2 million. He only succeeded in making a good election speech and I should like to do the same.
I also congratulate the hon. member for Rosthern (Mr. Nasserden) who asked this morning why we pass such acts as the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. I must tell him that if we adopt those measures which were introduced by the Liberal government, it is because the latter realized at the time that western farmers were in need of assistance. I can speak about this, because in 1931 I spent over 12 months in the province of Alberta. I also had the opportunity of visiting the province of Saskatchewan which was then in the grip of a terrible drought. It was following that drought that the Liberal government implemented those acts. I am willing to give the Conservative government credit for having introduced the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act but it is the Liberal party which has seen it through. We voted for it because we were aware of the western farmers' situation and we felt sympathy for them.
There seems to be some feeling that we are not justified to speak of the problems found in eastern Canada. I should not want to sound prejudiced but I think our present laws do not give enough protection to eastern farmers. Members from Quebec know that. If only they had the courage to say so. That is why I congratulate the hon. member for Rosthern who one day had the courage to express his views on certain agricultural legislation.
Last year I asked the Minister of Agriculture if he was thinking of extending the coverage of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act to other parts of Canada.
Here is what I said on this matter, on April 12, 1961, as found at page 3603 of Hansard (page 2 of the English translation), when I put the question to the Minister of Agriculture in these words:
Mr. Chairman, in connection with this item 36,
I wish to direct a question to the Minister of Agriculture, arising out of a statement he made recently to the effect that the Prairie Farm Assistance Act would be extended to the whole of Canada. Would he like to comment on that?

Supply-Agriculture
To which the Minister of Agriculture replied:
The Prairie Farm Assistance Act applies only to the prairie areas. The statement I made some months ago was that the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act should be applied to Canada as a whole because it is concerned with the rehabilitation of water and soil resources. I feel a similar type of act should be provided for the whole of Canada.
That was put on the official record last year. And I should like to ask the acting minister if it is the intention of the government to extend the scope of this legislation to all the provinces in Canada.

Mr. Chairman, I feel that I would be remiss in my duty this afternoon if I did not take part in this discussion concerning agriculture, and specifically this item on land rehabilitation, irrigation and water storage. I think it is well known to my colleagues and other members of the house that I come from a part of Canada which has had the recurring problem of drought. Even in my short life span I have experienced three of these serious drought cycles.
In commencing my remarks on this particular item I should like, first of all, to congratulate our present Minister of Agriculture on the very positive action he has taken in connection with this matter. I am referring to last year's drought as far as Saskatchewan and western Canada are concerned. It points up in effect how this government has taken a realistic view of some of the problems of agriculture. I wish to congratulate our government on their national agricultural program. In fact I can assure the committee that in the eyes of the agricultural population of this country this government is fast becoming famous through our Minister of Agriculture for their national agricultural program.
This agricultural program not only deals with the over-all problem but also with regional problems, and the item we are discussing this afternoon deals with a serious recurring problem of a regional nature that we experience in the west. I come from a part of Saskatchewan that has one of the highest cattle populations per capita compared to anywhere in Canada. Not only has it a high cattle population, but the quality of the cattle raised in our area is second to none. As proof of this statement I would point out that at a recent royal winter fair in Toronto at which I was a visitor, I discovered that there were 101 head of cattle which came from the province of Saskatchewan and had been selected by the livestock associations of that province. Out of the 101 head of cattle selected for exhibition purposes, 36 head came from the great riding of Moose Mountain. I am reminded that the balance came from Swift

Current-Maple Creek. I cannot assure the committee that this information with respect to Swift Current is absolutely authentic, but I do know they raise a lot of good cattle in Swift Current-Maple Creek.
The fact is that with these purebred, high quality herds water is naturally a very important factor in the economy of that part of the country. In the discussion today mention has been made of emergency fodder banks, and so on. This program is very important, but coupled with it is the emergency program of water conservation. I am thinking now of dugouts, small dams and also the emergency well drilling program that was put into effect last fall. This program was very timely and helped to maintain quite a number of basic herds in our area.
I was very glad to hear the Acting Minister of Agriculture, the Minister of Fisheries, mention that there had been at least 100 applications under this emergency well drilling program. I know that a number of them were from the riding of Moose Mountain. I might suggest in passing that like any other new regulation or emergency measure there were a few doubts about the plan, but it did work very well.
I make the following suggestion to the committee. Because of the great importance of water conservation to areas such as the one in which I live in Saskatchewan, I think that any way in which we can propagate the over-all development of P.F.R.A. should be considered on a permanent basis. The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar mentioned the south Saskatchewan dam. We feel this is the grand-daddy of the whole project of water conservation in the prairies and western Canada, and I hope to live to see the day when we not only have that dam completed on the great south Saskatchewan river but when we will have other dams along its tributaries and other rivers in Saskatchewan, and Manitoba for that matter, which will preserve the precipitation we have in the west which presently runs away through our streams into the oceans.
In my area of Moose Mountain, under the water conservation program that we are now considering in the supplementary estimates we have experienced the co-operation of the government. I should again like to take this opportunity to thank our Minister of Agriculture, and through him the cabinet, for the attention that has been given to the water shortage problem in my riding. I am referring to the assistance we have received in connection with a dam on the Souris river at Oxbow, Saskatchewan, which was completed a year ago. Also, an appropriation of $110,000 has been granted for a new

dam at Gainsborough, which happens to be my home municipality. In addition, according to information I have just received another appropriation has been allocated for a dam at Lightning creek, Redvers, and I understand that consideration has been given to building one at Maryfield. These are very, very important to my area. This program comes under this supplementary estimate and I know the constituents of Moose Mountain greatly appreciate the co-operation I have received from this government in regard to this very serious problem of water conservation.
I referred a moment ago to the emergency well drilling program. I discovered that in the application of this emergency legislation last fall there were a few criticisms with regard to the policy. One of them was that the farmers concerned thought the expenditure of $1,000 for the development of a well seemed to be unfair when it was decided to locate the well on one particular farm because it seemed to give that individual farmer an important benefit in comparison to the neighbouring farmers. The suggestion was made that perhaps the municipality, in conjunction with the province and with the agreement of the federal government, could make some provision whereby part of the cost of the well could be recovered from the farmer upon whose land the well was placed. If this suggestion were taken up, I think this objection would be overcome.
Another suggestion was made to me and I am in agreement with it. It was that we should not consider this just as an emergency well drilling program but should make it a permanent policy of, say three wells, every year in each municipality because under the present emergency provisions the municipality is allowed to drill three wells with government assistance at the federal and provincial levels. If this program were arranged in cooperation with the municipalities and the provinces to develop a well drilling program so that the cost could be spread over the next five or 10 years, a greater number of these emergency wells could be provided.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, we have lived through three or four serious drought cycles and we can expect to have them again in the future. Rather than have an emergency develop when we will find a shortage of water in areas where we have these very important cattle herds, if these wells were provided for now they would be there and it would eliminate any emergency which might develop in the future. This, together with our very accelerated P.F.R.A. dugout program, the small dams program and
Supply-Agriculture
water conservation program such as we have in the south Saskatchewan project, and irrigation, would I think, in the long haul eliminate one of the greatest bugbears affecting the agricultural industry in Saskatchewan. We know we have one of the most highly productive areas in the world as far as wheat production and top quality cattle are concerned. We have these recurring droughts which cause an emergency, such as we encountered last fall.
That is all the remarks I wish to make this afternoon. I would repeat that we appreciate this program. I wish to support the supplementary estimates because these programs are very important to our part of the country which has to suffer these recurring droughts.

Mr. Chairman, under the item for land protection, reclamation and development I wish that from some portions of my constituency I could help out the Saskatchewan farmers, particularly in the area of the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, that of Moose Mountain. We have a problem which is a little different. We have too much water; it comes off the mountain too quickly. I am referring specifically to the Similkameen river which is in my constituency. We have a similar situation on the Rock Creek river. These are both good sized rivers; in fact, I think they would make the Saskatchewan river look sick when they are in full spate. Briefly, our problem is that we have a high run-off, practically an uncontrollable run-off. We need federal and provincial help to tackle the engineering problem. I am hoping that ARDA, as its program develops, will have the answer.
Generally speaking, the agriculture policies brought in during the last five years have been excellent. We have felt their benefit in the Okanagan region the Similkameen region and over in the Grand Forks area just as, I imagine, people interested in agriculture have felt them all over Canada. It seems, however, that ARDA is in a state of flux at the present time. We know that a director has been appointed. Specifically, I should like the department to tell us at this time how far they have gone in the development of ARDA. Has the director met with the provincial ministers of agriculture, for instance? Have they developed a plan? In the case of British Columbia, have those concerned with this program actually got together or not?
To get back to the principal problem, the control of the Similkameen river presents a great many difficulties. I do not know whether the work would be undertaken by the provincial government in co-operation with the federal government and the local

Supply-Agriculture
authorities or whether it would be undertaken by one or other of those authorities, separately or in conjunction, but the solution of this engineering problem will not be easy. I think the work will in any case be expensive enough to warrant the federal government sharing the cost with the provincial and local authorities.
Referring specifically, once again, to ARDA,
I	have one more question to ask. Will this machinery be used in cases where a small area could be well served by the placing of a dam, and will it be used in conjunction with the work of provincial governments? What I am really doing is to seek information in order that, looking to the future, I may be able to advise my constituents how they can go about getting aid under the terms of this act.

I am sure all members of this committee were most happy that, after years of talking and promising, a federal government has been prepared to co-operate with a provincial government and bring into actuality the commencement of work on the south Saskatchewan dam. In the supplementary estimates which we are now considering under vote No. 616 there is detailed on page
II	an amount of $1,600,000 as the additional amount required in this fiscal year in connection with this scheme.
I wonder if the acting minister is now in a position to give the house a progress report on the south Saskatchewan project. Perhaps he could tell us not only what stage has been reached in the physical construction to date, but also something about the planning which has been done for the future. Important as agreement between the federal and provincial governments may be as far as the construction of the dam itself is concerned, undoubtedly one of the most vital factors is the planning for the utilization of the potential which will be made available in the areas of flood control and irrigation. Undoubtedly this will be an extensive phase of the new development of that area, and I have been wondering what proposals or agreements have been reached as to the method of developing the new irrigation areas and the sharing of responsibility between the federal and the provincial governments. I have been wondering also, whether provision is to be made for the giving of federal aid to the new areas during the formative years. These are matters which should not be left to the last few months. I think we would be most interested to know what information the minister can give us concerning progress made not only in connection with the dam itself but in respect to planning so as to utilize to the full the potential which this new project will

create. As I indicated, we would also be interested in the distribution of the cost and the amount of help which will be provided so that the people of this area may reap the fullest benefits in the shortest possible time.

Mr. Chairman, I cannot let pass unnoticed the remarks made by my friend the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger). I want to comment on them, not to start a controversy but simply to put the record straight.
A few minutes ago, the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska tried to insinuate that we, from the province of Quebec in particular, did not have the courage to give our opinion on the emergency measures for western farmers.
I want to say first of all, Mr. Chairman, that we are very happy to see our friends in the west benefit from legislation enacted to help them when their crops fail. I might add that when a similar situation occurs in eastern Canada, the same thing is done. As a case in point, I would ask my hon. friend from Drummond-Arthabaska to go back to the time of the hog cholera epidemic in my constituency and his last year; he will recall how quickly the federal Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Hamilton) took measures to remedy the situation.
My hon. friend from Drummond-Arthabaska surely remembers that some 400 herds of swine were affected and that it cost approximately $1,500,000 to the federal government to check the hog cholera.
I do not think we are doing either the eastern farmers or the western farmers a good turn by trying to stir up one group against the other.
I believe that we should concentrate our efforts and do our best in order that farmers may receive the same consideration, when they go through such hardships.
Since my hon. friend talked about the P.F.R.A. emergency fund, I would remind him that the western farmers had been contributing from 1939 to July 1960. They contributed about half of the amount paid back to them in grants.
Whenever a western farmer sells oats or grain of some kind, he is contributing to some extent to the emergency fund. I think we should give consideration to those factors and not raise a controversy, detrimental to both groups.
Let us join hands and we shall certainly succeed in giving satisfaction both to eastern and western farmers for neither the eastern nor the western farmers are seeking pure and
