I regret that the Minister of Agriculture is still sick as a result of his strenuous efforts on behalf of the farmer because my first remarks were intended for him personally. I wished to pass on to him words of appreciation from farmers in my constituency and other farmers as well for the assistance given last fall by the community pasture division of P.F.R.A. I refer particularly to the prompt action taken last autumn to establish an emergency feeding program. An emergency community pasture was set up in my constituency at Craven, as was mentioned in his opening statement by the acting minister. I visited this feeding ground several times last fall and talked to farmers who had cattle inside the fences on the 1,000 acres of crown owned grass and hay land on the Valeport flats. It was quite a sight to see the great herd in one pasture, many hundreds of head all together, but made up of small numbers from many farms. There were considerable quantities of water and pasture feed in the marshlands.
There was also the emergency feeding by pellets. These pellets made from grain screenings and molasses provided a balanced diet for the cattle. The pellets plus the available pasture feed produced highly satisfactory results. The pellets contained 11 to 12 per cent protein and 15 to 20 per cent fibre. This pellet feeding was provided to the cattle owners at a cost of 10 cents a day for a cow and an additional 4 cents a day for a calf. This nominal charge did not nearly cover the cost of the pellets and I imagine much of the $100,000 in this supplementary estimate covers the extra cost to the government.
As I said, I visited the pasture grounds on several occasions last fall. The farmers were very appreciative of the government's emergency program. One cattle owner said the gov-erment assistance was a godsend. He explained that he had been right out of feed and his cattle were eating weeds in the ditches along the roads when the emergency feeding program was announced.

I know the farmers were rather proud of the showing their cattle made, which was observable by motorists driving along the highway. There were always a number of owners helping with the pellet feeding and generally keeping an eye on the whole herd. When the nights were dark enough to offer an inducement to old time cattle rustling with modern equipment such as trucks, the owners took turns standing watch.
On one occasion when I visited there, 15 or 20 farmers were working together inoculating all the animals. Everyone seemed to be having a good time except perhaps the animals when the needles got a bit blunt.

Mr. Chairman, I am surprised at two things. One of them is the lack of vocal representation on behalf of the farmers of eastern Canada by their members. The second is the overabundance of apple polishing by members from western Canada. The charge is made today, and I think it is a justifiable one, that we as members of parliament should look at the estimates we are discussing in terms of what the government is doing and where it is going.
I am not particularly interested in the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre congratulating the minister on having done something for him personally. We are concerned with a program. I was given to understand that a great many of the abuses under P.F.A.A. had been done away with by the government, but that kind of apple polishing speech only indicates to me that the abuses have not been abolished and are coming back with a vengeance. I suggest that this is not what we want.
We should look at agriculture as a whole and I think we should be very surprised that a long range program instituted in the days of Bennett should apply only to three named provinces. Is this problem not a basic problem that affects all of Canada? Have some of the Conservative members not stood up and said that the long range program of their party and of the government is ARDA? Is ARDA not an extension of assistance to all the provinces and, if so, why has it taken so long to do something about it? In the pamphlet issued by the minister, which the hon. member for Timmins reminds me was issued to the public before the legislation was passed, there is this statement:
As a means of meeting the small farm problem the government has under consideration ways and means of improving the level of living of farmers on small farms by means of better land use, encouraging the formation of economic farm units.
The reference is to a statement by the Prime Minister as found in Hansard of August 30, 1958. On December 15, 1960, we passed legislation providing for the extension of these benefits to other areas of Canada. Can the farmers not legitimately ask the government why the benefits are not being extended to all Canadians? Why is western Canada alone benefiting? Is it not time that the Minister of Agriculture told the Canadian people why the legislation is not being extended to all parts of Canada? When ARDA was enacted the minister agreed, as I think every member of the house did, that ARDA was not going to be legislation for specific provinces but would apply to all agricultural provinces.

Let us not fool the Canadian people into thinking that this money is to solve the drought problem in western Canada last year. It is true that there is a little extra money and it is quite true that there have been a few more wells drilled but this legislation has been on the statute books of Canada for many years, in good years and in bad. Is it not true that western farmers are as well able to look after their ups and downs as well as other farmers are? If it is, then the pamphlet that was issued to sell ARDA is not correct. It is pointed out in the pamphlet that in the province of Saskatchewan, for instance, only 4 per cent of the farmers had annual production under $1,200 in value.

Mr. Chairman, this is not the ARDA program. I am reading from the pamphlet that was issued before the ARDA program was instituted. It illustrates what is needed in western Canada, and I can well understand the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs raising a point of order because here is an indication that in Saskatchewan only 4 per cent of its population had an annual income under $1,200 a year. In the province of Quebec the figure is 28 per cent.
We have absolutely no objection to and have always supported programs for western Canada. We are simply asking now that some of the western members be good enough to help some of us in the east to do for the rest of Canada what we are willing to do for them. We have provided the machinery that has made it possible, along with good government in Saskatchewan, for the people of that province to have better incomes than in any other agricultural province in Canada. The province of Quebec is one of the worst off in this regard and their problems are connected mainly with the dairy industry. All I am saying is that we should give the same kind of assistance to them and it can be provided under exactly the same kind of items as we are discussing today.
In my area there are thousands of acres of cleared grassland on which the farmers are not bothering to grow hay because they cannot sell it. We would like to have community pastures. We would like the government to come to us and say that they will feed our dairy cows for 10 cents a day and our calves for 4 cents a day. They are paying for this in the large area of western Canada affected by drought and are able to do it for $100,000. I think that the government is to be congratulated if this is the case, but I think the minister is under obligation to tell

us how much of the money went into the subsidy to pay for the pellets which the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre suggested were provided out of the $100,000.
I am only suggesting that if this is a good thing for the farmers of western Canada then let us not have it only in the years when there is drought. Any beef producer will tell you that if you can feed a cow for 10 cents a day you are doing exceptionally well. In fact, if you can keep a herd alive in my part of the country for 10 cents a head you are doing very well. I should like to know why this subsidy is not being provided under this program in my part of Canada and in the rest of the country. The Conservative members from eastern Canada must be aware of the situation. I know that many of them are connected with the dairy industry, which is in very serious straits. Good heavens, Mr. Chairman, surely we do not ask for legislation just to elect a large number of members from western Canada but rather for legislation which applies to all of Canada, which is good for all of Canada and which assists the agricultural industry to operate in the most effective and efficient way and to get the most out of the natural resource being used. If there is anything else being done under these provisions I think we should find out about it now. While the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs does not want to talk about ARDA, I thinly this would be a very good time for farmers all across Canada-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This vote is for an extension of what is an important hospital insurance principle for Canadian government employees and their dependants who are stationed abroad. It is for the foreign service and affects a total of 8,700 people. The position was that by a vote in 1958 treasury board was authorized to make regulations providing for hospital insurance for Canadian government employees and their dependants abroad, for dependants of the R.C.M.P. abroad, and dependants of the armed forces.
That was extended by the Appropriation Act of 1960 so that it would cover service subsequent to returning to Canada until these employees or their dependants could pick up the provincial plans. The basis of contribution is that which an employee would make were he resident in Ontario. In other words, this plan for federal employees is based upon the Ontario hospital insurance scheme. This particular supplementary estimate is to cover additional costs due to a considerable expansion that has occurred in the membership and the use of this plan since the preparation of the main estimates for the year.
In addition to the extension of the scope of the plan additional moneys are required so that members of the forces will not be without hospital insurance coverage while on certain types of leave without pay, or while qualified for coverage under a provincial plan having been released from the service immediately prior to or upon their return from a posting outside Canada. The amount previously voted was $130,000; this vote is $90,000, making a total of $220,000 for this purpose during the year.

Mr. Chairman, if the committee looks at the language of the vote it will perhaps realize that we are again carrying on this business of legislating under the estimates rather than by amendment of an act. The former member for Winnipeg North Centre has elaborated on this argument and I am not going to repeat it. Of course, his criticism in those days was directed to the

I know that Ontario has the largest population and, of course, has one of the oldest provincial governments.
Why do we rely upon Ontario as our standard for what might be made available to employees of the crown serving outside Canada, particularly when in an administrative way I think Ontario has not been very generous in these welfare measures, including this particular one of hospital insurance.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend surprises me greatly when he suggests that the Ontario plan is in any way niggardly. My personal impression is that it is the very reverse. I have had opportunity during the last two or three years to take advantage of the Ontario plan, and I must say I have felt it was a most generous plan in all particulars.
I am not in a position before the committee today to make a comparison between the amount an employee of the federal government might receive in one province as against another. 1 can only say to my hon. friend that it would not be feasible to have ten separate plans operating and use the residence or domicile of the individual. The only reason the Ontario plan is chosen, I think, is that the national capital is located in Ontario and it is thereby the most convenient plan to adopt. I am sure that all those who benefit by this plan are quite satisfied that they are receiving generous treatment.

There is one respect in which the Ontario plan is much less satisfactory than that of the other provinces. I refer to the fact that it does not cover the whole population. In British Columbia, for example, there is a sales tax and everybody is covered by hospital insurance. In Ontario it is true that all people employed for wages are covered, but self employed people are not all covered.
Only there are more than eight people in the firm.

Perhaps this is not the proper occasion on which to make this observation, but I believe that there is no more inefficient bureaucracy that I have discovered than the Ontario hospital insurance commission. I say that out of personal knowledge of a number of cases. They can take a good many lessons from the department of health and welfare here on how to organize a service properly. It may be that taking Ontario as

a model has no effect upon people overseas, and it may be I am using this committee as a forum for the expression of a grievance that I ought to get my member to express in the Ontario legislature. But my member in the Ontario legislature represents the riding of Russell and he seems to be otherwise preoccupied these days. You will understand me, sir.
Another question I wish to ask is this. The provision here refers to persons outside Canada, I take it, and it covers the period after their return to Canada before they would be dealt with under the operation of a provincial scheme. I think that in some provinces they would be covered as soon as they came back. In Ontario, as another of their little tricks, they deprive them of coverage for some time. But what I am trying to find out is this: does the federal government have any similar provision for any of its employees in Canada, or is this intended just to cover those who are not covered by any provincial scheme? For example, what about employees in the territories?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
This particular vote relates only to employees and their dependants abroad, or to dependants of members of the forces. With reference to the situation of employees in Canada, they will insure themselves under the various provincial schemes. I do have a recollection that there is a territorial scheme in existence both for the Yukon and the Northwest Territories. I am speaking from recollection only, but I believe the territories have arrangements similar to the provinces.
The federal government has in the last two or three years provided, on a generous basis, a group medical and surgical scheme which is an outstanding type of group scheme, though, of course, it does not involve the hospital arrangements we are discussing here.
As to the hon. gentleman's last remarks I can only say that my experience of the Ontario scheme has been very different from that which he has represented to the committee. I have found the Ontario scheme most satisfactory and most generous.

633.	Contribution to the New Brunswick disaster fund, $50,000.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to commend the government for this item. Perhaps I may be permitted to take a moment or two to say that this item seems to me to point up the need of a permanent fund of this kind to provide relief for our fishermen who so often have to suffer disaster. We all have poignant memories of the disaster for which this contribution is being made. A year before that there was a disaster in my own riding in which a dragger was lost with all hands as a result of which 14 families were left penniless. Only yesterday a storm occurred resulting in a loss of considerable property belonging to fishermen.

Supply-Finance
As far as I know no lives were lost but even the loss or destruction of property can be a disaster.
I wish to ask the government to give consideration to establishing a permanent disaster fund for fishermen. The minister pointed out some time ago that fishermen do not have too much in common with farmers. However, the farmer can always go to bed and sleep safe and sound every night but the fisherman risks his life every time he goes out to earn his living. I believe special consideration should be given the fishermen in view of that fact.
We have had ample evidence in recent years of the disasters which our fishermen and fishing communities have to suffer. I urge the government to give consideration to establishing a special disaster fund for fishermen.

634.	Grant to 1'association des universities de langue frangaise to assist in defraying the expenses of the first world congress of French language universities held in Canada in 1961, $15,000.
(Translation):

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words about this item whose purpose is to pay a grant to the association des universites de langue frangaise. It will assist this organization in defraying the expense of the first world congress of French language universities which was held in Montreal from September 9 to 13, 1961.
I should like to point out right now that this item comes under the government's program designed to foster the expansion, throughout the world, of the French culture, to which six million Canadians belong, in the same way as the federal government already promotes the cultural development of commonwealth countries.
The congress I mentioned was an essentially international event, because it brought together representatives from 37 universities where teaching is done exclusively or mostly in French. In addition, the governments of the ten states made it a point to be represented by observers, high officials of the national education or foreign affairs departments. Two countries even sent their minister of national education.
At the end of the conference, the participants established an organization which ensures close contact between the Frenchspeaking universities of the world and which will take the necessary steps and carry out proper investigations and research on their behalf.

The organization is known as AUPELF that is the association des universites en-tierement ou partiellement de langue fran-caise. Its board is composed of Msgr. Irenee Lussier, rector of Montreal University, chairman; Mr. Marcel Bouchard, rector of the University of Dijon, France and Mr. Mohammed El Fasi, rector of the Moroccan Universities, vice-chairmen. The members come in particular from Lille, France; Algiers; Liege, Belgium; Dakar, Senegal; Leopoldville, Congo; and Tananarive, Madagascar.
The fact that these members, who have chosen a Canadian as chairman of their association, come from such widely scattered places clearly indicates the international character of such a meeting and the worldwide importance of the role our Frenchspeaking universities are called upon to play.
In this respect, I hasten to remind the house that Mr. Andre Bachand, who has recently been appointed assistant to the rector of the University of Montreal, played a major part in the organization of the convention. I take this opportunity, Mr. Chairman, to congratulate Mr. Bachand for the work he has done on this occasion, as director of public relations at his university, and to congratulate him also on his recent appointment to his important post. The many members of this house who have had the pleasure of meeting him appreciate his courtesy and competence. They will join with me, I am sure, in wishing him every success.
May I also associate with these congratulations Mr. Jean Marc Leger, editorial writer of he Devoir. The success of the convention is largely due to him. On that particular occasion, he substantially contributed to the renown of Canada abroad.
In passing this item 634, the committee will acknowledge the advisability of giving aid to AUPELF whose work, let us not forget, will benefit many Canadians since this organization will stimulate co-operation between Canada and foreign countries through the exchange of professors, scholarships and courses for students and scholars, as well as through the exchange of textbooks and reference and scientific works.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to add my voice to that of the Secretary of State (Mr. Dorion).
He is very pleased that 1'association des universites de langue frangaise chose to hold its first convention in Canada. This adds to the importance, not only of the French culture in Canada, but also to our French Canadian universities.

I am sure all the members will be pleased to approve this additional amount, for everyone to know that in Canada, the Englishspeaking as well as the French-speaking Canadians gladly unite in order to assist association des universites de langue fran-gaise to go on in its efforts to make known throughout the world the French culture which is particularly appreciated by those who have taken the trouble to get acquainted with it.
I associate myself wholeheartedly with the Secretary of State in support of the item we are asked to vote on.
(Text):

I am sorry I must confine my remarks to English on this occasion as my French is not as good as the Prime Minister's. However, I want the committee to know we consider this a worthwhile move and are proud to be associated with any estimate that leads to a further development in understanding of the great French culture.

Hon. members will realize this amount refers to a conference already held. We all appreciate the honour that was given Canada when this country was chosen as the site of the first conference of the French language universities association.

Supply-Forestry
answer I gave to the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River in respect of the amount of $65,000. That actually is approximately the total budget of the organization. Item agreed to.
DEPARTMENT OF FORESTRY Forest research branch-
635.	Operation and maintenance-further amount required, $80,000.

I intend to be quite brief. The members of this group cannot resist having a few words to say on such an important estimate, one of $80,000 for additional costs in connection with the forest research branch, inasmuch as we realize how important this work is to the welfare of the present and future generations. The only thing we regret is that more is not spent on forest research. When you study the budgets of European nations and some other nations and consider the great importance of the forest industry to Canada, we are still not spending nearly sufficient on forest research if the work required is to be done. Before proceeding I wish to thank the minister for his courtesy whenever I have sought information or asked for bulletins or literature or things of that sort which are within the range of his department. I appreciate that courtesy and I appreciate also the minister's woodsy feel. You can be a technician; you can know the scientific aspects of forestry; but if you have not the woodsy feel-and it is something you acquire by living in the forests and being associated with the industry-you do not understand the problems as well.
I intend to have more to say on the main estimates. However, the importance of this work is not understood by many members of the house. I was just glancing roughly through the annual report for 1960-61 and I noticed that this branch is undertaking work in silviculture and management, mensuration-which is a very important subject, changing the techniques from one type of scale to another -tree improvement, tree biology, forest and forest land, forest inventories research and forest fire research. AU these activities require greater funds than have been available in the past if the work is to be undertaken satisfactorily, and in time to produce the results which are, shall I say required or necessary for the practical application of the recommendations derived from the studies in some cases.

Supply-Forestry
I rise at this time, particularly to draw attention to one aspect of forest research or the direction in which forest research can be applied. I wish to refer particularly to the work of the Canadian tree farmers associations. I urge the government to give that at present small organization, but one growing in importance, every possible assistance and encouragement. It is a socially responsible and desirable form of free enterprise as it is composed of persons who are aiming to accept their responsibilities to present and future generations by making certain that we conserve and develop our forest resources to the greatest advantage.
It is marvellous field for young people to enter if they wish to have a co-operative attitude toward life and yet have the opportunity to give expression to personal initiative and personal application of their abilities and energy. I therefore urge every consideration for this organization. Its main purposes are to promote the conservation and the development of forest resources through the ownership of woodlots and tree farms by individuals, small corporations and so on.
I wish to bring to the attention of the committee and the minister briefly the rec-commendations made by this organization to the resources for tomorrow conference, as they were the result of numerous meetings on the part of the directors in association with other persons who have been interested in this field. I might say that this forest industry is my life blood; I have lived my whole life in it. The recommendations are as follows:
(1)	An extension forester must be available eventually for every 100,000 to 200,000 acres of tree farm land and woodlots.
There is a connecting link between the tree farmer or wood lot farmer and the research facilities that are available.
(2)	In general to encourage competent tree farmers to remain in all areas of general marginal and submarginal food producing land and to encourage these tree farmers to hold or obtain adequate acreage to support a healthy tree farming activity in all such communities.
That is where a good deal of research is required in order to find out different types of land that are suitable for this purpose, and species that are less suitable. It is a splendid field for young people from rural communities, particularly if it is allied with farming or other rural activities. Then they go on to say this:
Complete desertion of these areas would result in less intensive tree farming in the entire area because of the alternative, less economical, less intensive operation possible by public ownership.
I agree with that statement, on that scale, They continue:

We must not adopt a policy in Canada that would unwittingly have the effect of creating collective, publicly owned farms of the type in Russia.
Then the next recommendation is as follows:
(3)	Availability of loans on long term at low interest rates to encourage and aid the independent tree farmer during a period of as much as 25 years to establish an efficient, productive, high yield tree farm.
I might say that 50 years ago I bought some land upon which nothing was growing but ferns, willow herb and willows. Now I have on that property white pine, 2 feet in diameter and as much as 100 feet in height. It is particularly good growing land, but it shows what can be done in one lifetime. From the point of view of the average Canadian where our forest resources have been so readily available, we have not acquired to any great extent to date that long term view or that willingness to plant at the present time for the benefit of future generations, which prevails to a much greater extent in Great Britain and in European countries. I remember that when the Duke of Buccleuch was here he told me what he had done on his estates since the war. To give him credit, may I say that his family has a sense of responsibility to the state and a responsibility to future generations. One hundred and ten thousand acres of his estate were overcut and in a sense destroyed because of the necessity to supply pit props for war production in the second world war. I forget when it was that he was here, but I think it was about four years ago. At that time he told me at the family's own expense they had replanted 77,000 acres. How many corporations have done that in Canada in the same period since the second world war, corporations that have no timber because in days past they destroyed the forest by their methods of logging and so on. I admit that those practices are changing and improving. However, I see a great future for the forest industry in rural communities. I am speaking on this item in view of the necessity of extending forest research because there are millions of acres in Canada which can be brought into production for the benefit of future generations and, with proper and selective cutting, can provide some income for the present generation. The association goes on to recommend:
4. Vocational training of tree farmers in the technical features of growing, harvesting and marketing of wood as a crop. This will be a form of adult education and may be copied from the Danish folk schools.
I might say, Mr. Chairman, that I have read a good deal about their practices, and I bring this to the attention of the Minister of Labour who I see is listening to what I have to say.

This is a type of vocational training that has not been undertaken to date and one that can be applied very successfully in a good many areas of Canada if you can get the cooperation of the local forest industry, the local educational authorities and local farmers' and other organizations. There is an opportunity here for the training of these people along vocational lines so that they will have the knowledge that will place them between the scientifically trained forest engineer and the person who works in the woods without knowledge of what he is doing. This is the next recommendation of the association.
5. The federal and provincial governments can assist our association greatly in carrying out its programs for local groups of woodlot owners by making available technical information on each of these programs and providing media for demonstrating this information to farmers at meetings. This could be the basis of the vocational adult education program. Macdonald college and other colleges have similar types of programs and others are needed.
I think these programs can be fitted into vocational schools. I am very glad to see that a vocational school is going to be erected in the city of Nelson as a result of the cooperation of the federal and provincial governments. Here is an ideal centre. As you know, Mr. Chairman, in my constituency alone last year there were over 300 million board feet of lumber cut and I believe it is estimated that up to 400 million board feet of lumber a year can be harvested in perpetuity by selective cutting. When you think of that vast and perpetual production and the increasing necessity for skills and for understanding in the industry and the increasing part that tree farmers or woodlot owners, whichever you like to call them, can play, one can see that there is a tremendous opportunity here.
In British Columbia the tree farms are largely huge areas that are leased by the large corporations from the provincial government. When I speak of tree farmers I am speaking of those who have anything from 100 to 5,000 acres of timber which they are operating on a perpetual yield basis. I should like to suggest that in establishing vocational schools the Department of Forestry would be very wise to get in touch with the industry and enter into consultation with all those people who have a knowledge of forestry and forest research including departmental officials and the local institutions in the area it is intended to serve. We can establish these vocational training schools for the management of tree farms or woodlots, and we have a lot of marginal land which will provide an opportunity to arrest the drift, shall I say,
Supply-Forestry
toward the entire destruction of what I term socially responsible and socially desirable free enterprise.
In the district in which I have spent the greater part of my life and which is a forested area, the harvesting of timber is largely carried on at present by three corporations. Yet there is a tremendous opportunity for the use of marginal lands with co-operation between the federal and provincial governments in making possible the purchase of forested land for tree farm purposes, the promotion of tree farming and the provision of opportunities for literally thousands of persons to have independent, happy and fruitful lives by the practice of this occupation.

Mr. Chairman, if I may say a few words following the spokesman of the free enterprisers and the dukes, I should like to say that I too cannot find it in my heart to suggest that we should not vote at least this additional sum for the purpose for which it is requested, that of forestry research. I wish to make a special appeal, and the minister will understand readily why I am doing so, for the intensification of research into two particular aspects of forestry. After all, our forests provide the biggest and most valuable crop in Canada, a fact that is sometimes forgotten, and it seems to me that we lose a great deal of that crop every year by fire. This was particularly brought to our attention, of course, by the forest fires in Newfoundland last summer.
It seems to me there are two kinds of research that could very well be intensified. The first is research into better and also cheaper methods of fighting fires because, as I discovered, fighting fires is not a job for enthusiastic amateurs. To be done successfully it has got to be done by people who know how.
It is true, of course, that forest fires are not always a total disaster, that there are times when forests benefit from being burned, but in most cases it is desirable to arrest these fires at a very early stage. I recognize that in this field most of the responsibility rests with the provinces, but the federal government can certainly do a good deal in two directions, first, by the co-ordination of efforts and perhaps the establishment of a strategic reserve of firefighters and, second, by research into better methods of fire fighting.
There is another aspect of this subject which it seems to me also deserves constant study, that of salvage after a fire has taken place. We know that in most cases these fires do not destroy everything and that a great deal can be salvaged if the right methods are used. A great deal can also be done if

Supply-Forestry
the right methods are used to promote the healthy development of new forests where fires have taken place. Perhaps because my own constituency was more adversely affected by forest fires last year than any other single constituency in Canada, the matter is possibly more in my mind than it is in the minds of some of the other hon. members at the present time. The minister came down himself to see what was happening at the very height of our difficulties last summer and I am sure I am addressing a minister who is very sympathetic. The minister, like the hon. member for Kootenay West, is familiar with the lumber business and, if I may say so modestly, I too have some knowledge because actually I was in the lumber business before I was 15 years of age. So that it is not just something in which I have taken an interest since I became a member of parliament. I feel that I am speaking to someone who is thoroughly sympathetic when I make this plea for intensification of this aspect of research, not that it is more important than the other aspect but because it is a field in which there is still a great deal to be learned, as is the case in every branch of the industry.
We do know that there is increasing competitiveness with woods products from products of some of our resources that are not renewable like the forests, and it is tremendously in the national interest to keep our forest products competitive in every way with other products, and not merely to keep up the supply but to increase the supply as the years go by because the demand will inevitably increase.
(Translation) :

Mr. Chairman, I am quite willing to associate myself with the hon. members for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) and for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), the latter being the most capitalistic of socialists, to say that there is certainly-I said socialist capitalist-and in order to join in their praise of the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Flemming).
The effort to instil into the public the importance of our future forests, and the forestry work to help the provinces were needed and called for.
I have been told, though I am no expert in this matter, that the minister is doing a remarkable job for which he deserves to be commended.
Earlier today I heard the hon. member for Kootenay West tell us that he once planted trees that are now 135 feet high, and measuring several feet around the base.

As far as I am concerned, in 1942 I went into the bush to fetch two spruce trees which I took home and planted in front of my house. I looked after them, 1 saw to it that they were not broken, and, today, those trees have reached a height of about 35 feet, and a diameter of about 12 inches above the roots, whereby, that means if someone, even without being an expert in the matter, makes an effort to study the question, he finally loves all that beautifies the surroundings of his home.
In 1936, we made a test in Hull. We obtained from the provincial government of Quebec, for the junior chamber of commerce of the city of Hull, 1,200 maple trees which were transplanted in that city. Unfortunately that work had not been preceded by a period of education and preparation of our school children. Those 1,200 maple trees were planted but, unfortunately, there are only three or four left today, because they were broken by the school children who ran and played around them, not being used to such means of adornment and embellishment in our cities. Thus the city of Hull was deprived of a desirable improvement because one of those maple trees planted near my place has now reached about 100 feet in height and a diameter of some 18 to 22 inches at the butt. If we had first of all had our school children fully understand the value and beauty of trees, they would have protected them and today our city would be so much the nicer with 1,200 fine trees.
Therefore, I would ask the minister to enter into an agreement with the departments of education of the various provinces in order that an educational program be implemented to instil into our children and our young people the beauty of a tree and its value around private homes, and in the forest.
I do not believe the minister will refuse to consider that matter which in my opinion is of the utmost importance because the growing generation is not adequately prepared in that field.
When the Department of Forestry was created some time ago, we complained that the minister had not appointed a single French Canadian to an important position. Now I see here the item "salaries and wages" and I feel I may ask the minister if he has been able, since the establishment of his department, to find at least one person from the province of Quebec or from any other part of Canada with a thorough knowledge of French to act in an important capacity in that department. Because, as I said some time ago, some English speaking people, probably without any ill will, ignore the fact that there is a very touchy French speaking group in

Canada-and one cannot blame them for being touchy. We have always been a minority, and we are still considered as such except in the province of Quebec which some seem to be treating as some kind of a reservation- French Canada-the province of Quebec only.
Well, I think we are entitled to be touchy and to ask, each time the occasion arises, what we are entitled to in Canada.
I am making this speech without any acrimony or spitefulness. But I ask this: if it has not already been done, I hope the matter will be reconsidered, and that it will be realized that the French element was entitled to be represented in that department, because we do have in Quebec forestry experts.
I know that, for some time, the Quebec government has been picking senior federal civil servants to bring them over to Quebec. Well, we could do the same thing, and pick within the provincial civil service a certain number of experts whom we could bring here in Ottawa; we would then establish the required balance, which would make French Canadians happy, as they are entitled to be.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ELECTORAL DISTRICTS IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES
speechtext:
I intend to do that, Mr. Speaker. The bill is one which in its present form seeks to amend the Representation Act and there are certain consequential amendments to the Canada Elections Act. At the outset I should like to explain that I do not ask the house to pass the bill in its existing form. I will be asking, with the assistance of my hon. friend from Chapleau, for certain amendments to be made which would have the effect, not of adding a member to this house for the Keewatin and Franklin districts of the Northwest Territories but rather of adding those two districts to the existing electoral district of Mackenzie river, thus giving the residents of the Keewatin and Franklin districts the representation which thus far they have been denied.
Before I explain those changes I wish to very briefly emphasize the reasons which urge this house to give second and final readings to this bill before the house rises to attend the royal assent to certain bills which Your Honour has indicated will occur at 15 minutes to six o'clock.
First, and most important, is the fundamental concept that in a free democratic society such as ours in Canada, every adult Canadian is by law clothed with the right to take part in government and to vote for representatives who govern. This basic concept was set out clearly in the four kinds of rights to which the United Nations dedicated itself in the universal declaration of human rights in 1948, a declaration which grew out

of the public demand for advancing the inherent and equal rights "of all members of the human family".
Second, and of paramount importance in all the circumstances, is the protection afforded to all Canadians by the Canadian Bill of Rights. Since the passage of that act there can no longer be any excuse for continuing to deny to any Canadian the human rights and fundamental freedoms of Canadians wherever they may live in Canada and without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex.
Third, I do not think any member of this house would take issue with me when I say that it would be a dangerous practice indeed to perpetuate the policy of King George III of England of taxation without representation. This is precisely what has been happening to some 8,000 northern and Arctic Canadians for more than half a century.
Fourth, I submit to the house that it might perhaps be prudent, in terms of Canadian sovereignty, to enfranchise our northern and Arctic Canadians before the Russians do so.
In short, this bill which I propose, with the assistance of my hon. friend from Chapleau, to amend by these proposals which I intend to explain in committee of the whole should, I submit, be allowed immediate second reading for these four very compelling reasons. In summary, it would eliminate the long standing denial of the franchise to some 3,000 to 4,000 northern and Arctic Canadians. Second, it would eliminate that discimination with which the Canadian Bill of Rights concerns itself. Third, it would eliminate the abhorrent practice of taxing Canadians without their right to be represented in parliament, and fourth, it would strengthen our northern and Arctic sovereignty.
The essential principle of this bill-for the benefit of my hon. friend from Skeena-is quite simple: it is to extend to those Canadians living in the Keewatin and Franklin districts of the Northwest Territories that which is their undeniable right, the right to vote.
At the time of introducing this bill I thought this would be best achieved by providing for an additional member of this house to represent these two districts. Since introducing the bill on January 22 last, however, the territorial council of the Northwest Territories has been meeting in Ottawa and has passed a resolution calling for the consolidation of the existing three districts of the Northwest Territories-that is, the Mackenzie, the Keewatin and the Franklin districts-into only two districts divisable, approximately, by the northerly extension of

the 102nd meridian which divides Manitoba from Saskatchewan.
It is contemplated that this division, to occur in 1964, will result in each of the two districts having its own territorial council. I should also explain here that this is a further urgent reason for extending the franchise to the resident Canadians of Keewatin and Franklin in that they are not even represented on the existing territorial council of the Mackenzie River.
It is at this time, I submit-that is, in 1964 -that consideration might be given by parliament to the addition of a new member. In other words, the circumstances have changed since I originally introduced the bill of January 22 on the basis of a resolution passed by the territorial council of the Mackenzie District, Northwest Territories.
In the result, therefore, the amendments to this bill which will be proposed in committee of the whole will eliminate that aspect of the bill which would require the addition of a member of parliament to represent these two districts of the Northwest Territories. Instead the two districts concerned, Keewatin and Franklin, would be added to the electoral district of Mackenzie River, thus enfranchising those Canadians resident in Keewatin and Franklin.
I have available over 100 copies in English and in French of the reprinted bill as proposed to be amended in committee of the whole. I will ask, Mr. Speaker, that these be distributed to hon. members immediately upon going into committee of the whole. I have also attached to the bills a copy of maps in English and in French to assist hon. members during their consideration of this measure in committee.
There is a degree of urgency about obtaining both second and third readings today. As all our members are aware, if the bill does not pass through both second and third readings today it will go to the foot of the list and is not likely to come up again this session. Since this session will probably be the last before a general election, this would mean that these Canadians affected by this measure and entitled by law to the vote would once again be denied their rights as electors. I am sure no hon. member of this house would wish to delay the passage of this bill in those circumstances and, in the result, be the cause of perpetuating the disfranchisement of these northern Canadians. In addition, and this is most important, the chief electoral officer of Canada must be given the opportunity to erect the necessary election machinery in the areas of Canada concerned.
Representation Act
In urging the co-operation of all hon. members in giving an immediate second reading to this bill so that we may go into committee of the whole to consider the proposed amendments, let me say that for some time I have been urged by citizens groups such as the Baker Lake citizens association in the Keewatin and the Mackenzie River Progressive Conservative association to obtain recognition by this Canadian parliament of the fundamental rights of all qualified Canadians to representation in this house. I therefore urge all hon. members to allow the bill to go immediately to the committee of the whole for consideration of the proposed amendment.

I rise to indicate what I would have indicated with reference to the previous bill, except for the reference to the act which was repealed. I wish to assure the hon. member for the Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) of our support for this measure. We approve the desire to give to a group of people, no matter how small or how large, the right to representation in the House of Commons.
Hon. members will recall that one of the first things I sought to do upon taking my place as a member of this house was to accomplish substantially the same thing with respect to native Indians in Canada, that is, to give them the right to vote in federal elections. That idea subsequently took the form of legislation. We in this party have always supported any attempts to give the people all possible rights to representation in

Representation Act
this house, and, naturally, we have no hesitation in supporting the bill which is before us.
I note that one provision of the bill- indeed, it is one of the principal parts of the measure-relates not to the Representation Act but to the Canada Elections Act. I think this was necessary because of the nature of the area referred to in the bill and described by the hon. member from the Yukon. This provision seeks to give the chief electoral officer of Canada the right to appoint more than one election clerk, as I read it at a quick glance. This provision is necessary, as I see it, to ensure that it may be physically possible to operate the machinery of the Canada Elections Act so that everyone in the area has an opportunity to vote.
Apropos of this subject, there is another matter which we might consider. It is not only the returning officer and the various election clerks who will have difficulty in covering the area properly and seeing that the machinery of the Canada Elections Act can operate effectively. I think we must direct our attention to the vast size of this area and consider making the changes necessary to ensure that the elected representative of that region together with those who may be candidates can receive some assistance from the public treasury in order that they may have the opportunity to travel across this vast territory which, according to my memory, is more than a million square miles in extent. It is a tremendously vast area, and I think we should consider establishing the principle that the public treasury may assist candidates to ensure that the message gets across to these people in a political way. Otherwise we may end by giving them only the right and the opportunity to vote in elections without providing for that sense of attachment to the candidate or to political situations which is possible in urban areas.
We are happy to support this bill and the request of the hon. member for the Yukon. We shall do everything possible to facilitate the passage of the measure.

I think this will be an appropriate point for me to comment on the point raised by my friend the hon. member for Skeena and subsequently referred to by my friend the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. I also have a fairly comprehensive experience in travelling over vast areas in the north. I might say that the situation has been vastly improved in recent years with the advent of the D.E.W. line, mining activity up there and the oil and gas exploration and activity in those areas. There are now many more air flights made into the Arctic islands and into the northern Arctic areas of Canada generally than were made formerly. It is not an insurmountable difficulty now, so the chief electoral officer assures me, to set up the necessary election machinery, provided of course there is sufficient opportunity before an election is called, or no more than there would be in most areas of the Mackenzie river district.

Representation Act
I should also say, in respect of travelling in these two districts, that there are roughly 15 administrative centres where there is a population concentration which is entitled to vote and these 15 administrative centres are serviced fairly regularly. With this type of communication improvement it seems to me that it should not be too difficult for the member who might subsequently represent the district to hitchhike rides from one portion to the other in the discharge of his obligation to represent his people. I might also point out one further factor, namely the greatly improved radio communication in those areas which allows that sort of communication.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE ELECTORAL DISTRICTS IN NORTHWEST TERRITORIES
speechtext: The explanation of the hon. member as to the relative ease that exists now as compared with conditions a few years ago with regard to getting around a district such as this is welcome news. I have a constituency which is considered to be large in itself but which, compared to this new district, is one quite easy to deal with. While I can appreciate that it might be easy to hitch hike rides, as the hon. members says, through a district which has more square miles than two provinces put together, I think the matter will not be quite that simple. I am still interested in the concept that the public treasury should take account of the geographic features as between ridings and should pay an amount additional-and perhaps this will be done by way of differentiation-to the indemnity which members now receive. May I say this provision would not be confined to the Northwest Territories but would I am sure be applicable to the constituency which the hon. member represents, the constituencies of Port Arthur or Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador or to my own and that of others whose territory is over the 1,000 square miles mark. I am not raising this matter in order to be critical of the bill, as on second reading I indicated our support for it. What I am now suggesting would be something which the hon. member could not introduce in any event because it would require a money bill and consequently could be introduced only by a member of the cabinet. In any event, this is a factor which I think must be considered in future years in order that a member would have reflected in his sessional indemnity the geographic factors with which he is obliged to contend and the high costs of transportation. Having done some hitchhiking through the northern part of my constituency I myself have discovered that hitchhiking is not always free, but that sometimes it is costly as well.

has prevailed throughout the day, he could find it in his heart to give us at least a general indication of what the government's program will be for the whole of next week.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I would gladly enter into an agreement with the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate and I will give the program for the entire week if he will announce the subject of the supply motion which will be debated on Monday and Tuesday.

Mr. Speaker, the seductive invitation of the hon. gentleman is of course entirely subversive to all the rights of an opposition and is not one that I could entertain; but I can assure the hon. gentleman that my conduct will be characterized by that spirit of co-operation which I always show in the house, and I hope he will respond to my invitation.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: On Thursday and Friday we will follow with estimates, the likelihood being that the further supplementary estimates which were not finished today will be taken up on Wednesday. Whether or not some legislation will be introduced, I cannot say at this moment.
And there will be a supply motion on Monday?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Oh, yes.
